title: Environmental and genomic associations of inter-annual and inter-tree variation in acorn production in pedunculate oak
content:
Abstract
Many plant species exhibit masting, the geographically synchronous, highly variable annual production of seeds. This behaviour is thought to have evolved in diverse taxa and ecosystems as a strategy to enhance pollination success and overwhelm seed predators, with far-reaching ecological consequences. In temperate forests, masting in oaks (Quercus spp.) shapes forest dynamics and restoration outcomes, but the mechanisms driving acorn yield variation among individual trees within a population remain poorly understood. We quantified mature acorn production over 4 years in 38 Quercus robur L. trees in Wytham Woods, UK, and tracked earlier reproductive structures shed using litter traps over three years. Acorn production varied widely among trees and years (CV = 125%): approximately one fifth of ‘super-producers’ contributed disproportionately to half of the total acorn crop, a dominance less pronounced during the 2020 mast event. Acorn maturation, not flower number, explained interannual variation, consistent with resource-based fruit abortion strategies hypothesized for oaks. Open canopy conditions and less-developed spring leaf canopies were the most robust correlates of higher mature acorn yield, while sandy clay loam soils reduced early acorn abortion. Exploratory genome-wide association analyses identified 2306 SNPs associated with reproductive output and environmental variables, with candidate genes enriched for disease-response functions. These results highlight the complexity of reproductive strategies in long-lived trees, shaped by environmental and genetic factors. Understanding these dynamics is crucial for predicting forest reproductive output and improving seed sourcing for woodland conservation and climate-adapted restoration.
